title: The pancreas: two organs in one
objective: Distinguish the exocrine and endocrine pancreas and match each islet cell type to its hormone.

steps.title: Exocrine: the digestive factory
steps.body:
Most of the pancreas is **[[exocrine]]**: it secretes into ducts, not blood.

- **[[acinar cell|Acinar cells]]**, clustered in grape-like acini, make digestive enzymes: proteases such as trypsinogen, plus amylase and lipase.
- **Duct cells** add a bicarbonate-rich fluid.

The mix drains through the pancreatic duct into the [[duodenum]].

visual.alt: Left: an exocrine acinus, a ring of acinar cells full of enzyme granules draining into a duct toward the duodenum. Right: an endocrine islet of beta cells in the core and alpha and delta cells at the rim, with a capillary carrying hormones into the blood.
visual.caption: Exocrine acinus (left) secretes into a duct; an endocrine islet (right) secretes into blood. The islet shown is mouse-style, with beta cells in the core.

steps.title: Endocrine: the islets
steps.body:
Scattered through that tissue are the **[[islet|islets of Langerhans]]**. They make up only about 1–2% of the pancreas, and they are **[[endocrine]]**: their hormones go straight into the blood.

- **[[beta cell|β cells]]** → insulin
- **[[alpha cell|α cells]]** → glucagon
- **δ cells** → somatostatin
- **PP cells** → pancreatic polypeptide

steps.prompt: Match each pancreatic cell to what it releases.
steps.explanation: Islet cells release hormones into the blood; acinar and duct cells release digestive juice into ducts.

steps.prompt: What makes a gland *exocrine* rather than *endocrine*?
options: Exocrine glands are simply larger than endocrine glands
Exocrine glands secrete into ducts; endocrine glands into the blood
Exocrine glands are under nervous control, endocrine are not
Exocrine glands only ever make proteins, nothing else
steps.explanation: The definition is about *where* the product goes: a duct (exocrine) or the bloodstream (endocrine). The pancreas does both, from different cells.

variants.setup: A gland can be exocrine or endocrine.
variants.prompt: What makes it exocrine rather than endocrine?
options: Exocrine glands are simply larger than endocrine glands
Exocrine glands secrete into ducts; endocrine glands into the blood
Exocrine glands are under nervous control, endocrine are not
Exocrine glands only ever make proteins, nothing else
variants.reveal: The definition is about where the product goes: a duct or surface (exocrine) versus the bloodstream (endocrine).

steps.prompt: Acinar cells make proteases as inactive [[zymogen|zymogens]] (trypsinogen rather than trypsin). Why?
options: Inactive enzymes travel faster through the pancreatic ducts
It stops self-digestion; they're activated only in the duodenum
Active enzymes simply cannot be stored inside the cell
Zymogens are much cheaper for the cell to manufacture
steps.explanation: Trypsinogen is switched on in the duodenum (by the gut enzyme enteropeptidase), and trypsin then activates the other enzymes. When activation happens too early, inside the pancreas, the gland injures itself. That is a central idea in pancreatitis.

variants.setup: Acinar cells make proteases as inactive zymogens (trypsinogen, not trypsin).
options: Inactive enzymes travel faster through the pancreatic ducts
It stops self-digestion; they're activated only in the duodenum
Active enzymes simply cannot be stored inside the cell
Zymogens are much cheaper for the cell to manufacture
variants.reveal: Keeping enzymes inert until the duodenum protects the gland; activation too early, inside the pancreas, is a key step in pancreatitis.

steps.setup: In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys β cells while the acinar tissue is largely spared.
options: Digestion fails, but blood glucose stays completely normal
Blood glucose rises with no insulin, while enzyme output is kept
Both digestion and glucose control fail completely together
Nothing changes, because α cells simply take over the job
steps.reveal: Losing β cells removes insulin, so blood glucose climbs. The exocrine factory, about 98% of the organ, keeps making enzymes. The two halves of the pancreas can fail independently.

flag.note: Exocrine function can also be reduced in diabetes; the point here is that the two compartments are distinct.

variants.prompt: In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys β cells but largely spares acinar tissue. What do you expect?
options: Digestion fails, but blood glucose stays completely normal
Blood glucose rises with no insulin, while enzyme output is kept
Both digestion and glucose control fail completely together

variants.explanation: Losing β cells removes insulin (glucose rises); the ~98% exocrine pancreas keeps making enzymes — the two halves fail independently.

flag.note: Exocrine function can also be reduced in diabetes; the point here is that the two compartments are distinct.
